title: Can you call yourself a leftist?
body:
My friends and I had a debate the other night about leftism as personal identity/lifestyle vs. leftism as collective political practice. I am someone who personally identifies as a leftist. However, it has become apparent to me that if you come from a background of privilege and eventually work a corporate job, it isn’t in your discretion to retain the title of a leftist. A true leftist would devote their life to their belief and cause. A true leftist would refuse to work for The Man in order to live in a commune. A true leftist wouldn’t sit around debating all day, they would go outside to advocate and work on legislation and policy! But a true leftist also wouldn’t work in policy because that is progressivism and liberalism, and not true leftism.

I claim all of this. I have been the person to work for The Man, I have debated political theory, and have sat around all day, sitting and agonizing with these thoughts. But I have also worked on policy that benefited working class San Franciscan residents. However, I am also someone who is financially stable and has endless support from my family and those around me. I will never know what it is like to struggle at the hands of capitalism and be at my wit’s end. I will never know what it is like to feel intense pressure to survive and build wealth in a world that is working against my attempts to do so. But ultimately, I maintain my stance and my belief. I claim the title of leftist.

If leftist, why not devote your life to leftism?

This is purity politics in its most essential form. Political belief does not require total lifestyle change. This argument is individualist and falls onto a liberal framework. Your personal career choices should not bear the burden of systemic change, that is the responsibility of our collective action. Leftism is not martyrdom. It should also not necessitate martyrdom. Limiting your options or purposely impoverishing yourself to relinquish all privilege in an effort to prove your sincerity ironically turns leftism into a movement accessible only by those who can afford to make that sacrifice. Arguing against leftist sincerity because one’s career isn’t their cause is confusing political identity with vocational identity.

The idea that you must be uncorrupted of capitalism in order to hold legitimate political views is a deeply individualist and almost Protestant notion that connotes salvation through personal virtue.

Structural privilege enables leftist belief.

This is true; I live within financial flexibility which allows me to indulge in these beliefs–the system itself will not completely destroy my livelihood. But, does this mean that only those without privilege can be authentic leftists? Should the people who come from stable families wait until they are financially independent in order to participate and engage politically? Isn’t that doing less, and not more?

Historically, the left has never actually been a movement of people that have fully exited capitalism. That is quite difficult to do, considering the current political and economic state of the world. In fact, navigating mainstream institutions while maintaining critical consciousness is closer to an organic intellectual (Gramsci) than vanguard purity politics.

Why not be someone that contributes something to the world then? Be a teacher or food bank worker!

Agree, those jobs are unbelievably admirable and generous. But if we really get into the technicalities, working at a food bank is structurally, a quite conservative act. The fundamental purpose of food banks is to patch the wounds that capitalism opened, while also not actually threatening the system that creates them. By making inequality more bearable, it also makes it more sustainable.

Teaching on the other hand: a very, very noble profession. But schools as institutions are, according to Gramsci and later by Althusser, ideological state apparatuses. In essence, they are mechanisms through which capitalist hegemony is passed on and transmitted to the next generation.

In fact, Althusser specifically argued in his essay Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses, that schools have replaced the church as the dominant ideological state apparatus under modern capitalism. Schools as institutions naturalize existing power relations and teach children to accept their place in the division of labor, effectively reproducing the conditions of capitalist production. Thus, if we go by this framework, teachers are functionally closer to priests of the existing order than to revolutionaries. This “teacher” argument is one that is ignorant to the most foundational leftist analyses of what teaching truly does structurally.

However, radical teachers do exist! Genuine leftist teaching appears more so as critical consciousness and challenging naturalized hierarchies. It’s teaching students to question before fully accepting. However, this specific practice is separate from the inherent function of the teaching profession.

We can continue on, and on, and on about all of these particular jobs that one could take over a capitalist or corporate career in order to be authentically leftist, but these jobs that people continuously bring up are based on aesthetic and cultural association. This argument is feelings-based rather than one of political conviction.

My point on working within capitalism.

In One Dimensional Man by Marcuse, he observed that advanced capitalism developed the ability to absorb opposition by turning it into a consumable aesthetic. Radical posturing, such as looking and performing radicalism, was one of the ways that the system neutralized genuine critique. Performing leftist authenticity through lifestyle choices is how capitalism defangs dissent by making it into an identity product.

Engels also, in Socialism: Utopian and Scientific, argued against the tendency to construct ideal communities and pure positions outside of existing society; for example, communes or separatist communities. This is what he called utopian socialism. According to him, this was sentimental and politically useless as it simply avoided the actual mechanisms of capitalist power rather than confronting it directly. A very good example of this is Henry David Thoreau’s Walden! His great experiment in radical self sufficiency was, the entire time, being subsidized by his mother doing his laundry and providing him with home-cooked meals, and land in the forest owned by Ralph Waldo Emerson, and provided free-of-charge for Thoreau.

However, these arguments force my hand at discrediting the work of food bank volunteers, teachers, and theorists who want to share their thoughts with the world.

Ultimately…

Leftism itself is a political consciousness and alignment. It should not be a lifestyle purity test or a constant need to prove your leftist sincerity. All jobs under capitalism are capitalist by definition, and this dissolves the moral hierarchy in which people construct between “good” and “bad” jobs. Critical consciousness, sustained belief, intellectual engagement, doing what you can with what you are able, are all legitimate and very meaningful forms of political practice. It is imperative that privilege be acknowledged in the flexibility of people following leftist ideology, as well as the inflexibility of those who must work tireless capitalist jobs for survival, but these acknowledgements should not be used to disqualify someone’s political alignment because privilege is a structural condition. We must be clear-eyed about difficulty and unbroken in commitment!

Many of my friends have nowadays succumbed to defeatism. But, I still believe that changing consciousness is still deeply valuable and matters significantly, even if I won’t live to see the outcome. Mark Fisher said that it is easier for us to imagine the end of the world before the end of capitalism. This pervasive atmosphere of inevitability is exactly what makes sustained belief feel naive and opposition feel futile.

However, if everyone internalizes capitalist realism and surrenders belief, then the self-fulfilling prophecy essentially fulfills itself. I strongly believe I will not see the end of capitalism. I think most, if not all, of the people around me would agree with this statement. But the difference is between those who give into defeatism, and those who hold open the possibility against the weight of everything trying to close it. This, here, is why I choose to retain my title of leftist.

title: Our Ascent into Techno-Feudalism
body:
“Once upon a time,” Marx and Engels wrote in The German Ideology, “a valiant fellow had the idea that men were drowned in water only because they were possessed with the idea of gravity. If they knock this notion out of their heads, say by stating it to be a superstition, a religious concept, they could be sublimely proof against any danger from water.” The man, they note, spent his entire mortal coil trying to cure humanity of this delusion, certain that by banishing the thought of gravity, he’d be able to abolish the fall itself. And his doctrine survives today in a new form.

Our widespread and general belief that material conditions can be overcome by the right idea now appears nearly everywhere: in billionaires who promise that we will reach emancipation and freedom from exploitative labor relations through software, in policymakers who outsource social crises to predictive models, in techno-spiritual evangelists who insist we are one update away from utopia, and even in everyday users who are convinced that their contradictions can be optimized away by better apps or products. The valiant fellow has simply multiplied; he now lives in each of us as we continue insisting that the ideal can override the material, that reality can be debugged if we just write the right line of code or use and implement the most efficient data structure. This is what Marx called ideology.

Marx provided us with an antidote for ideology: dialectics and historical materialism. He anticipated that material contradictions would eventually force capitalism to collapse in on itself. Instead, capitalism learned to reroute those contradictions, and what we are seeing now is capitalism with reorganized architecture: a change from industrial production to computational extraction. Surplus is now made with data and the owners of these oligarchical data and AI platforms occupy positions that seem to resemble feudal sovereignty far more than democratic enterprise.

Guy Debord’s Society of the Spectacle, Jean Baudrillard’s Simulation and Simulacra, and Michel Foucault’s Discipline and Punish, are of the utmost beneficence within this context. Taken together, this paper argues that these works provide the analytical tools through which we can understand how contemporary technological and AI systems reorganize agency, power, and knowledge in ways that allow capitalism to persist through mutation instead of collapse. In what I describe as our ascent into techno-feudal society, archaic, feudal structures return under the veneer of innovation, and positions owners of computational infrastructures as the new lords of digital territory, all while enclosing cognition and leaving users dependent and increasingly governed by systems they never get to see.

As written in The German Ideology, Marx and Engels believed that history advances through the tensions between material forces and our social relations. Time and again we have seen the coming and going of varying modes of production: primitive communal societies (egalitarian groupings and kinship-based organization), slave economies (ancient Greece and Rome), feudal lords (medieval Europe, parts of Asia, land-based economy), owners of capital (industrial revolution and onwards). Each of these carried a contradiction that would eventually result in its reshaping. However, for capitalism, the contradiction had been forecasted to be between labor and capital. As capitalist exploitation intensified, class consciousness would subsequently grow, and thus, the system would rupture, causing socialism to follow suit. But even through society’s current and supremely uncanny resemblance to what’s coined as “late-stage capitalism”, the end is far from near; the aforementioned linear transformation into communal living and shared resources appears as though it may never materialize. Instead, what we are seeing play out before us now, is capitalism avoiding its demise by absorbing the crisis into itself. Wage stagnation gave birth to debt markets, social discontent resulted in branding and lifestyle and identity politics. Each of these contradictions now presented an opportunity for reinvention.

Now, in 2025, we are seeing in full effect the forces of production abandon their industrial roots; they have become computational, and the primary supplier for surplus in this case, is data. This is our ascent into techno-feudalism.

A vocabulary is essential for understanding this transition. It helps to clarify and grasp what appears to be happening to reality and power. Debord, Baudrillard, and Foucault each offer conceptual tools that, albeit, when read together are fairly bleak, but are ultimately quintessential for thinking critically about what is to come. The theories do not all align and perfectly agree, but they fall along the same ideas, such as how agency is dissolving into simulation and how power is dissolving into infrastructures.

In Society of the Spectacle, Debord’s most largely heralded line claims that “the spectacle is not a collection of images, but a social relation among people, mediated by images” (Debord 4). Debord presents the spectacle as something that reorganizes the very structure of how we interact with and relate to everything and everyone around us, rather than as something we simply look at. Images stand between us and mediation becomes social relation. In this sense, the spectacle operates through representation; images reshape how individuals understand both themselves and others, while also subtly constraining the forms of agency available within that mediated world.

Social media’s intrinsic purpose was meant to strengthen connection and communication. Nowadays, users on social media produce content (“images”) as a currency; an attempt to embody signifiers of desire. Platforms encourage individuals to craft and piece together idealized versions of themselves that are calibrated to what others would want; yet the more that those signifiers are chased, the more disconnected we, the people, become from ourselves. What ends up getting lost here is agency understood as the capacity to define our own desires independently, as individuals become more and more susceptible to orienting their self-presentation around algorithmic feedback. This mirrors Todd McGowan’s Lacanian account of “ the desire of the Other” in his book Capitalism and Desire: “The capitalist subject constantly wonders which object is the [...] most desired by other subjects. [...] We desire what we assume the Other desires because the Other desires it and because we want to attract the desire of the Other.” This way, image replaces relationship.

Modern algorithms exacerbate this cyclic phenomenon: the more curated the image, the more feedback it generates; the more feedback it generates, the more it feels like desire; and the more it feels like desire, all the more we long to chase it.

TikTok’s For You Page, Instagram’s Explore tab and recommended Reels are but a few examples of how the spectacle is “the self portrait of power” (Debord 24). We see what power wants us to see; we relate through specifically curated feeds and branding scripts. Power owns the means of mediation, and mediation is now the structure of social existence.

But, this has been our reality for quite some time now, where images mediate our relations. The reality we are approaching, however, can be explained through Baudrillard’s Simulacra and Simulation. He details what happens when mediation actually goes beyond mediating, and replaces our reality altogether. Baudrillard writes that we now witness “the generation by models of a real without origin or reality: the hyperreal” (Baudrillard 1).

Baudrillard claims that simulation is “the substitution of the signs of the real for the real itself” (Baudrillard 2). Agentic AI (e.g., Perplexity’s Comet, OpenAI Agents mode) isn’t necessarily severing us from the world, we have our physical laptops in front of us, we use our fingers to type, scroll, click, receive. But, what changes with agentic AI is actually the level at which interaction occurs.

With agentic AI, we give up the autonomous acts of searching, comparing, reading, deciding, and calculating. In a Forbes article elaborating on Perplexity’s Comet browser, Steven Wolfe Pereira explains that “[agentic AI applications] complete complex, multistep tasks without constant human intervention” (Pereira). In place of our own selves, we allow the AI to perform those cognitive acts on our behalf. The device on which we prompt the AI remains tangible to us; the world remains accessible; yet our relation to it is now mediated by a model that interprets reality for us before we even get to encounter it. Even in earlier forms of digital life, interacting with technology still meant engaging with the full texture of information. We sorted through endless emails, carefully read through long articles and were able to recognize a distinct and authentic voice, booked flights with lots of frustration and deliberation, and added items to our calendar because we wanted to remember them. Though these interactions were not necessarily “authentic” in a typically romantic sense, they required attention to detail, patience, as well as interpretation. In order to perform these acts, we were made to move through the world with some friction, and that friction is exactly what contributes to defining and creating meaning. It reflects a process of co-production; meaning and subjectivity emerge through sustained interaction between people and technologies rather than being instantaneously delivered.

Agentic AI removes all of these micro-encounters; it compresses writing and extracts structure. Ultimately, we are presented with the “essence” without an understanding of the time or interiority that created it. The model is the first encounter, and we become spectators of the agent’s engagement, all while removing ourselves as participants in our own.

Nevertheless, in a world where productivity is a condition of survival, it’s understandable that people may wish for tools that can streamline tedious tasks. When labor markets punish patience and the slowness of process, or when academic environments reward perceived merit and consistent output, automation offers a breather. And wanting that kind of relief is not to be mistaken as, or interpreted as moral failure. It should be seen as a structural failure.

The danger here is the slope of automation’s trajectory; automating what’s tedious, to automating the interpretive, to automating the relational, and finally to automating the self.

Many engagements benefit from offloading and streamlining. But others, such as reading or thinking, lose so much of their fundamentality when a model performs it for us. It ultimately prevents us from being able to see the world with our own eyes before the simulation ends up handing its conclusion down to us.

Agentic AI interposes an optimized version of the world that steadily and gradually becomes the only version we engage with.

We turn to Foucault to see how power runs underneath all of this. According to Foucault in Discipline and Punish, power is diffused through institutions, and exercised through practices of classification and surveillance. Knowledge allows us to arrange the world so that certain actions or behaviors can be governed.

Another dimension of techno-feudal power can be seen in the growing dependence on AI as an intermediary for knowledge itself. Students are encountering information through AI platforms that are able to summarize and reorganize material on behalf of textbooks or teachers at an exponential rate. In Discipline and Punish, Foucault describes the concept of “docile bodies”. He writes, “A body is docile that may be subjected, used, transformed, and improved” (Foucault 136). The contemporary student is now shaped by interfaces that streamline thinking and agency to perform interpretive labor to the point where intellectual work becomes almost entirely indistinguishable from compliance. Efficiency can be interpreted as neutral or even benevolent, but it ultimately produces what Foucault would call a docile epistemic subject; something that is predictable and easily guided.

When AI outputs appear authoritative and credible, the user never really sees the exclusions that structure them. Foucault claims that “power and knowledge directly imply one another” (Foucault 27), essentially meaning that whoever gets to control or own the production of knowledge also controls the formation of subjects, which is why the increasing reliance on AI is dangerous. A model update can alter political assumptions or change what counts as credible evidence, all while these changes remain unbeknownst to the public.

Another of Foucault’s central insights: “the individual is not to be conceived as a sort of elementary nucleus [...] it is one of the prime effects of power” (Foucault 29). As students turn to AI summaries and syntheses, their habits of thought start to match the exact structures that the system provides. The subject that thus emerges is one that is molded through convenience; someone that learns to think in the formats that AI makes easiest to access.

When the production of knowledge becomes automated, the production of judgment follows closely behind. In a system ruled by techno-feudal power, the same platforms that mediate the truth also get to determine where each person stands within the hierarchy they create. Foucault writes, “the examination [...] established over individuals a visibility through which one differentiates and judges them” (Foucault 184).

In education, AI graders and plagiarism detectors transform assignments into streams of data. Students get parsed as patterns or anomalies, rather than being truly evaluated as a thinker, or for the value of their work. Each submission would theoretically add another data point that situates them within categories that the system itself created. This exact same process governs workplaces using systems like keystroke monitors or productivity dashboards. And because this examination enforces and produces the subject that it judges, individuals internalize these categories long before any actual explicit evaluation gets to occur. The process is essentially performative; people pre-optimize their behavior and learn to match the preferences of the system that classifies them. They are hence shaped by the visibility that surrounds them, and AI platform owners get to define the terrain of knowledge and the terms by which subjects navigate it.

However, the theories only matter insofar as they touch the ground. The ascent into techno-feudalism creeps its way into various nooks and crannies, with each small shift revealing just how much power has begun to consolidate behind all of the systems we’ve come to consider as neutral.

Palantir renders this movement concrete. It presents itself as a neutral data processor, claiming to produce “products for human-driven analysis of real-world data” (Palantir), all the while its platforms modify entire categories of knowledge. Palantir’s own systems have been enlisted by the United States government and outsourced to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for “workplace raids, large-scale enforcement operations, and investigations involving asylum seekers—showing how Palantir’s pattern-finding capabilities have long been central to ICE’s most aggressive tactics” (Hubbard). Palantir outrightly produces classifications such as “risk,” “threat,” or “suspicious activity” and these classifications become a mechanism of power, they act as the lenses that authorities see through to police citizens; governance through anticipation. People behave very differently when they know every movement or association is logged somewhere, and is fed into a model that they never actually get to see. What emerges is a form of authority that feels atmospheric and inconspicuous rather than direct. This is power that operates in the way that Foucault warned modern institutions would operate; by scaffolding what you might do before you even get to do it.

This same logic applies to San Francisco’s newest private K-8 institution, Alpha School. Alpha School markets itself as a place where academic tasks are handled in just two hours a day by AI so that students can spend the rest of their time learning life skills and participating in creative activities like designing or owning a food truck (Buller). There is intuitive appeal here; digital literacy is undeniably essential now, more than ever, in our world where information is provided through interfaces rather than books, and having the ability to navigate technological and computational systems will become imperative as our society becomes more and more datafied.

But for young and highly impressionable children who are just beginning to develop cognition, having their first exposure to knowledge be mediated through an AI system that summarizes and curates for you risks turning learning into another form of software assistance. Children who never get to struggle through a textbook or article unaided or never experience confusion that only personal effort resolves, will develop a worldview in which insight is believed to be something that is simply fetched and not built. This is not to be interpreted as a hysterical objection to technology however; children should learn to interact with AI. But before learning how to delegate thinking, children should first and foremost learn how to think for themselves. Otherwise, the owners of AI will go beyond building educational software and begin to formulate the conditions through which learning is experienced. Digital literacy without intellectual literacy does nothing for the greater good of society if it only produces subjects who know how to use tools but not how to resist them.

When the map precedes the territory long enough, people start to mistake the map for the world.

Through historical materialism, Marx assumed that we would arrive at resolution through rupture. But capitalism had a different idea; it discovered recursion by learning from its own failures and finding new domains from which to extract value, foreboding our ascent into techno-feudalism.

The danger of this is how cognition itself is becoming enclosed. Ultimately, when all interpretation and judgment are delegated into opaque infrastructures, our autonomy unwittingly erodes right before our eyes. This requires all of convenience and asymmetry of ownership, and none of conspiracy.

In an effort to mitigate this trajectory, we must insist on cognitive literacy before delegation and public accountability over privately governed infrastructures. Education must teach how systems work before we allow or ask students to rely on them, and platforms that mediate reality must be subject to democratic scrutiny, rather than treated as tools that are neutral for all. Autonomy and human agency are cultivated; if they are not actively protected, they’ll eventually be optimized away.

Digital infrastructures are not inherently corrosive. But who owns the means of cognition and who controls the frames through which truth is filtered must be accounted for and held responsible. Otherwise we put ourselves at risk of recreating the valiant fellow’s delusion; believing that by creating systems and interfaces that are more and more efficient we can abolish gravity. But the fall remains, it just now happens inside systems that insist it is flight.
